Lingaraja Temple

11th century CE

The great Shiva temple of Bhubaneswar, which scholars call the most notable temple in Odisha. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2,3]

For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi: 'by far the most notable temple not only of Bhubaneswar, but also of Orissa'. Brown: 'the finest living example of the Orissan group'.

Dynasty
Somavamshi (Kesari) Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]
For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi treats 'Kesari' and 'Somavamshi' as the same kings. He says the side halls were later additions, possibly of the Ganga period.

Date
11th century CE Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2,3]
For curious grown-ups

Brown: c. 1000 CE. Panigrahi: 11th century, most probably begun c. 1020–1040 CE and completed c. 1040–1065 CE. No foundation inscription is known; the dating is stylistic and indirect.

Shiva as Tribhuvanesvara (Lingaraja) Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]
Temple type
pancharatha deul Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]

Meet the temple

The pieces that make it up, from base to top.

At first the temple had only the tower shrine and its porch. The dance hall and the offering hall were added later. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1,2]

Panigrahi explained that a temple's chief god came to be seen as living like a king. So the god needed an audience hall, a dance hall and a dining hall. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]

According to a temple chronicle, a queen had the eastern part of the temple rebuilt. Panigrahi thought she was Queen Kolavati, mother of Uddyota Kesari, and that she most likely built the porch hall. Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [2]

For curious grown-ups

The chronicle (Madala Panji, as quoted by Panigrahi) names her Tulavati Rani, wife of Vasukalpa Kesari. Panigrahi calls it 'most probable' that she was Kolavati, the builder of the Brahmesvara temple, and says she was the queen of Yayati II. Both steps are his inferences.

The main temple rises straight from the ground, with no high plinth (raised base) under it. Panigrahi contrasted this with the Parvati temple, which stands on a high plinth. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]

Why was it built?

The story behind it.

The temple stands in a very holy area. Percy Brown noted that the many temples in and around Bhubaneswar show how sacred this place was. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [3]

No known inscription names the builder. Historian K.C. Panigrahi thought it most likely that King Yayati II began it and his son Uddyota Kesari finished it. Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [2]

For curious grown-ups

This is one scholar's inference, not proven. Panigrahi (1961) dates Yayati II c. 1020–1040 CE and Uddyota Kesari c. 1040–1065 CE, and calls the attribution 'most probable'. He credits Yayati I with the Mukteshvara temple, not with Lingaraja. Some popular accounts name Yayati I instead; no accepted source for that has been checked.

Historian K.C. Panigrahi thought this temple replaced an older temple on the same spot. Some early sculptures in the courtyard may have come from that older temple. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]

According to tradition, King Sasanka built an earlier temple at this shrine in the 7th century CE. Panigrahi could not identify which temple that was. Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [2]

For curious grown-ups

Four Sanskrit texts credit Sasanka with a temple in this shrine. Panigrahi accepts that a stone temple stood here in the early 7th century CE. He dates the present temple to the 11th century and says the earlier temple cannot be identified.

How did they build it?

Stone, tools and centuries-old methods.

James Fergusson noted that the tower is built wholly of stone, from base to top. He also wrote that every stone in it has a carved pattern. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1]

The tower is hollow inside. R.D. Banerji saw rooms stacked one above another, reached by a stair built inside the thick wall. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]

The temple stands in a walled courtyard about 158 m by 142 m (520 by 465 ft). The thick outer wall is made of laterite blocks. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2,3,4]

Look closer: the wow details

The details worth a second look.

Today Lingaraja has all four buildings of a fully developed Odisha temple: the tower shrine, the porch hall, the dance hall and the offering hall. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [3]

Many smaller shrines crowd the courtyard around the main temple. Percy Brown compared this to Buddhist shrines grouped around a great stupa. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [3]

Panigrahi wrote that the temple dominates the landscape for miles around. He called it the purest example of the Kalinga style of building. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]

When Ganga kings later remodelled the temple, they added some features linked to Vishnu. Panigrahi noted these are not found in other Shiva shrines. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]

Its temple family

Other temples that shaped its design.

Panigrahi found the main shrine closely related in design to the Brahmesvara temple. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2]

Panigrahi wrote that later Ganga kings tried to match or outdo the builders of Lingaraja. They built even grander temples at Puri and Konark. Percy Brown noted that Puri follows the same four-building plan, in one line. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2,3]
